note: Vol. I No. 26, and the most legible issue of the month: page 3 column 5 carries eight Chicago advertisements almost unbroken, which is why the succession at the east end of South Water Street, the Pierce & Abbott dissolution and Giles Spring's corner address are all read here rather than from the three earlier issues, where the same notices survive cut. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST in this issue. Where a phrase is supplied from another issue of the same month the claim names that issue, its page, its column and its lines.

claims.notes: THE EAST END OF SOUTH WATER STREET CHANGES HANDS, AND THE PAPER SAYS WHOSE STORE IT WAS. Peter Cohen advertised himself at the '[E]AST E[N]D OF SO[U]T[H] WATER-ST[RE]ET' in the Democrat's very first issue (1833-11-26, claim c015, read from the scan-verified record), and this notice puts Doty & Co. in that same building from 29 April 1834. That is a succession chain of the kind the reconstruction can actually use: one identified frontage, two occupants, a date between them. THIS IS THE FULLEST OF THE THREE READINGS THE MONTH CARRIES — the same advertisement is cut narrower in 1834-05-14 (page 3 column 4, lines 2901-2915, where only 'CO. have taken the Store at' and 'of South' / 'Water-street,' survive) and in 1834-05-21 (page 3 column 4, lines 2683-2685). It was read here and cited there. The word 'lately' before 'occupied' is supplied: the line reads 'occupied by Peter Cohen' with its left edge cut, and the sense of a store TAKEN by a new firm requires it; nothing else in the notice dates Cohen's departure.

entities.role: partner, and the one who continues the business

claims.notes: RULING 3'S VETO, AND THE SUCCESSION THAT SURVIVES IT. The firm of Pierce & Abbott is dissolved on 5 May 1834, so the partnership does not stand in the 1835 town — but the notice says in the same breath that 'the business will be continued at the old stand by Asahel Pierce', so the SHOP does. The claim carries `contradicts` against the partnership and names both men. THE OLD STAND IS NOT LOCATED HERE: no street, no anchor, no neighbour — only 'the old stand', which is a placement the reader of 1834 could resolve and this corpus cannot. Asahel Pierce is the town's blacksmith in the later literature and this is the earliest notice in the corpus that names his partner, Titus H. Abbott. The same notice is cut narrower in 1834-05-07 (page 3 column 3, lines 2822-2834) and 1834-05-21 (page 3 column 4, lines 2724-2738); the surname reads 'si. aBBorr' in the first of those and 'TITUS H. ABBOT' here, which is what settles it.
claims.contradicts: the co-partnership of Pierce & Abbott is dissolved by mutual consent on 5 May 1834, the business continuing at the old stand under Asahel Pierce alone

claims.notes: WATER LOTS, SOLD AS SUCH, IN THE MOST BUSINESS PART OF THE TOWN. This is the wharfing question of the 1833 ordinance (1834-01-07, claim c003 — 'leaving eighty feet for a street') seen from the market side fifteen months later: the ground between the lots and the river is a distinct and saleable class of property called WATER LOTS, and twenty-five to fifty town lots, many of them water lots, are being auctioned on 20 August 1834. WHICH lots is not said and no block or street is named, so nothing is placed on the plat from this claim; what it establishes is that the category existed, was traded, and sat in the town's business quarter. The figure reads 'enty-fire to fy' in the transcription of 1834-05-14 (page 3 column 2, line 2739, 'wenty fee to TOWN LTS') and '“enty-fire to fy TOWN LOTS' here; twenty-five to fifty is the reading, and the alternative 'twenty-five to forty' cannot be ruled out from these two lines alone.

claims.notes: A SCHOOL HOUSE THE TOWN'S VOTERS ARE CALLED TO MEET IN, AND A SCHOOL DISTRICT WITH TRUSTEES AND A CLERK. The district's number is cut away — the line ends 'School Distriet A' — and is NOT supplied; 'No. 1' is bracketed as a supply and should be read as unresolved. What the notice establishes without any supply at all is that in May 1834 Chicago had a school house standing, a school district organised under trustees, and P. Pruyne signing for them. It sits beside the first issue's notice of a school 'recently established in this village, by Mr. Sproat of Boston' (1833-11-26, claim c003) and the infant school examined in 1834-05-07 (claim c001 there) — three separate schooling references in six months, none of them yet placed on the plat. The dateline reads 'Alay 97, 1851', which is May 27, 1834: the issue is dated 28 May 1834 and the year is impossible on a paper that began in November 1833.

Kinzie the corpus already carries. Long reference lists like this one are the forwarding trade's credit note and are transcribed here because the correspondents name the route Chicago's freight actually travelled.

Four readings of the same card survive in the month and every one of them destroys the signature differently — '2. I. GABLI' (1834-05-07, page 3 column 4, line 2988), 'Be Ba Sa4Rre' (1834-05-14, page 3 column 5, line 3024), 'Be Bo SAB!' (1834-05-21, page 3 column 5, line 2971) and this one. NO NAME IS ASSERTED. Carli relinquishes 'the tavern known as the Eagle Hotel' to J. Shrigley on 1 September last, 'during the term he continued the business'. claims.notes: THE TOWN'S BUILDING MATERIALS, PRICED, IN ITS OWN NEWSPAPER — and the numbers are the one thing this transcription will not give up. The 'CHICAGO PRICES CURRENT, reported for the Democrat by P. F. PECK' (page 3 column 7, lines 3145-3146 of this issue, and 1834-05-07 page 3 column 6, lines 3178-3180) runs its commodity names down one segmenter column and its figures down the next, and the figure column survives as '1 8 3 00 - 3.25 / 4 00 • 5P00 / 5 00' and nothing else. So what is claimed here is the CATEGORY LIST and its units: in May 1834 Chicago bought assorted poplar lumber by the thousand feet, shingles, square timber by the length, brick by the thousand, stone by the perch, lime by the barrel and wood by the cord. That is a statement about what the town built with and how it was sold, and it is worth a card even with the prices lost. THE PRICES ARE NOT SUPPLIED — the three surviving figures cannot be attached to a named row without guessing which row they sit against, and the row order of the two columns does not align line for line.

Daniel Elston & Co. announced the Chicago Soap and Candle Manufactory in the paper's first issue (1833-11-26, claim c030); this card, dated 15 February 1834 and still running in late May, says they have fitted up a smoke house for hams, bacon and beef. That is a second, differently-shaped structure on the same account — a smoke house is a small, tall, closed building with a distinct roof, and the reconstruction can say one stood at Elston's from February 1834. The words 'Smoke House' are supplied from the fuller reading of the same card in 1834-05-21 (page 4 column 2, line 3585, 'y have fitted up.a Smoke House,'), which is why they are bracketed here. claims.notes: RULING 3'S VETO AGAIN, AND AGAIN THE STORE OUTLIVES THE FIRM. Brewster, Hogan & Co. is dissolved on 20 February 1834; the claim carries `contradicts` against that partnership so it does not stand in the 1835 town. John S. C. Hogan continues at the old stand, and he is the same J. S. C. Hogan the corpus already carries as Chicago's postmaster at the scene date (1835-07-01, claims c001-c003) and as the man selling cedar posts in this same month (1834-05-21, claim c006). Two Brewsters are named, William and Franklin; SAME SURNAME, DIFFERENT FORENAMES, so they are two people and this project never merges those. THE OLD STAND IS NOT LOCATED — no street, no anchor, in either of the month's two readings of this notice (the other is 1834-05-21, page 4 column 3, lines 3636-3655).
claims.contradicts: the co-partnership of Brewster, Hogan & Co. was dissolved by mutual consent on 20 February 1834, the business continuing at the old stand under John S. C. Hogan alone

The card is dated 26 November 1833 and was read out of that issue as claim c020 there — 'MAT[T]HIAS MASON & CO. … on Main-street, nea[rly] opposite Graves['] [Tavern]'. This reading, from the last issue of May 1834, confirms the placement independently and gives 'opposite Graves' Tavern' where the 1833 reading had 'nearly opposite'; the qualifier is present in this month's other reading (1834-05-21, page 4 column 3, line 3703, 'oa, on Main-street, neasly') and cut away here, so 'nearly opposite' stands as the fuller form. GRAVES'S TAVERN AS AN ANCHOR is the point for the reconstruction: it is the house the Board of Trustees met in on 4 December 1833 (1834-01-07, claim c001), and it is what a smithy's address was measured against. MAIN-STREET IS READ AND NOT INTERPRETED — the name appears in two independent issues of this run and in the 1833 read, and this pass does not attempt to map it onto the platted grid.
